title: Low-effort AI-generated pull requests drain maintainer review capacity
statement: Popular open-source projects report a sharp increase in AI-generated pull requests and issues submitted without understanding or follow-up. Reviewing and triaging them consumes scarce maintainer time, and some projects now restrict or close outside contributions entirely.
affectedUsers: Maintainers and moderators of popular open-source projects (evidenced: tldraw, Rust, Astropy, LLVM, Linux, Ghostty, scikit-learn, Zulip, Godot)
severityNote: High. tldraw auto-closes all external PRs, Rust maintainers call it a DDoS on capacity, and several projects threaten bans.
frequencyNote: Recurring across at least 9 projects' policies and issues (Nov 2025 – 2026). A study counted 281 AI contribution policies in popular projects. No direct measurement of inbound volume was retrieved.

title: Compromised maintainer credentials ship malware in popular packages
statement: Attackers who gain a maintainer's registry account, publish token or branch write access publish malicious versions of widely used packages. The 2026 cases include a remote access trojan via axios and a credential stealer via litellm. The maintainers are victims, not insiders.
affectedUsers: Maintainers of popular packages and every downstream consumer
severityNote: Critical: RATs and credential stealers in packages with very large reach.
frequencyNote: At least four distinct incidents in the 2026 signals (axios, litellm, asyncapi, TanStack).

title: Fabricated AI-generated security reports waste triage capacity
statement: Security teams receive confident but fabricated vulnerability reports generated with AI tools. Each one must be investigated with priority, which pulls maintainers away from real work. curl no longer runs a bug bounty because of the incentive for made-up reports.
affectedUsers: Security teams of widely used open-source projects
severityNote: High for affected projects (curl removed its bounty), but evidenced by one origin only in this run.
frequencyNote: Unknown. Secondary reporting could not be retrieved in this session.

title: Minor and patch releases break dependents' code
statement: Package managers install minor and patch updates automatically on the promise that they're backward compatible. When a library breaks that promise, downstream projects break without warning. Users report pinned versions, broken release pipelines and lost weekends.
affectedUsers: Developers and teams depending on npm packages, and maintainers of libraries built on other libraries
severityNote: High when it happens: broken builds and pipelines, and emergency pinning.
frequencyNote: Hundreds of GitHub issues are titled about it. True frequency not yet measured.

title: New releases are installed before malicious ones are detected
statement: Automated and manual installs pick up new versions immediately. Malicious releases are typically detected and removed within hours, but not before they've been installed. Users ask package managers for release-age delays.
affectedUsers: Application and CI pipelines consuming open-source packages
frequencyNote: Popular feature requests on bun (693 reactions) and npm (241).

title: Submission effort no longer signals contributor trustworthiness
statement: Open source used to treat the effort of submitting a change as a signal of a potential long-term contributor. AI tools make plausible-looking submissions nearly free, so maintainers lose that cheap filter and are moving to explicit trust mechanisms that risk excluding newcomers.
affectedUsers: Maintainers, and genuine first-time contributors who face new barriers
frequencyNote: Articulated by LLVM, Vouch/Ghostty, tldraw and Astropy.

title: Trusted publishing can't be bootstrapped on npm
statement: npm's OIDC trusted publishing can't be used for a package's first version, so maintainers must still create a token or publish manually. That keeps long-lived credentials around.
severityNote: Medium: a narrow gap, but it keeps tokens in circulation.

title: Existing semver checkers only see the type surface
statement: The available and emerging checkers compare TypeScript type declarations. Many real breaking releases come from behaviour changes or from package metadata (e.g. a raised Node engine requirement), which those tools don't inspect.
affectedUsers: Maintainers relying on automated checks, and especially packages without TypeScript types
severityNote: Medium: a gap in tooling, not a direct harm.
frequencyNote: All four real complaints examined were non-type breaks (small sample).
